text: AI can optimize for almost anything. The question is: do you know what you want it to optimize for? Say you're using AI to design a new flight path. You could measure speed, on-time arrival, and fuel efficiency. But what about passenger nausea? Pilot fatigue? Trust in your airline after a turbulent ride? There are metrics you're measuring. And metrics you may be ignoring that might matter more. Before you prompt, before you build, or before you deploy, you need to define your win function. What does "good" actually mean for this specific use case? This matters more now because AI agents are coming - agents and systems that take your goal and autonomously figure out how to hit it. They'll optimize relentlessly for whatever target you set. If your definition of good is incomplete, the output will be too. And at that point, it's not the AI's fault. It did exactly what you asked.
